sec10-card-r02.teaching_text: Overtaking a cyclist and immediately cutting right across their front wheel causes a classic right-hook collision.

sec10-card-r03.question_text: Why do wet, sandy, or gravel-covered roads require extra caution around bicyclists?
sec10-card-r03.teaching_text: Skinny bicycle tires lose traction and slide out much faster on loose grit or rain-slicked asphalt than car tires.

sec10-card-r04.question_text: Who else besides walking pedestrians should you scan for behind your car before backing out?
sec10-card-r04.teaching_text: Bicycles move much faster than walkers along curbs and driveways, entering your backup zone in a split second.

sec10-card-r05.question_text: Besides hand and arm signals, what rider body cues warn you a cyclist may be about to change lanes?
sec10-card-r05.teaching_text: Braking or rough pavement sometimes keeps both hands on handlebars, making a rider's head turn your earliest clue.

sec10-card-r06.question_text: How do large commercial trucks and buses compare in size and agility with passenger cars?
sec10-card-r06.teaching_text: Heavy rigs cannot swerve or dart out of trouble quickly, so passenger drivers must leave extra operating margin.

sec10-card-r07.question_text: How do the blind spots around commercial trucks and buses compare with those of everyday cars?
sec10-card-r07.teaching_text: Long trailers and high cabs create deep blind zones on all four sides where entire cars disappear.

sec10-card-r08.question_text: In what three everyday driving actions do large commercial vehicles need extra space or distance?
sec10-card-r08.teaching_text: Heavy cargo weight resists both braking and building speed while long wheelbases sweep wide around intersections.
sec10-card-r08.must_match_memory_hook: Longer stops, slow starts, wide turns

sec10-card-r09.question_text: Why might a truck or bus swing into a left lane right before making a right-hand turn?
sec10-card-r09.teaching_text: Long rear trailer wheels track inward tighter than front cab wheels and would mount the curb without swinging wide.

sec10-card-r10.question_text: Why must you wait behind a right-turning truck rather than sneaking into the open gap beside the curb?
sec10-card-r10.teaching_text: As the cab swings right, the trailer closes that curbside pocket like scissors in the driver's blind spot.

sec10-card-r11.question_text: How does stopping fully behind painted intersection stop lines help trucks and buses?
sec10-card-r11.teaching_text: Creeping past the white bar blocks the front corner space cross-street semi-trailers need to complete tight turns.

sec10-card-r12.question_text: What should you do when waiting to turn left if you cannot tell how fast an oncoming truck or bus is closing?
sec10-card-r12.teaching_text: Large vehicles often look like they are moving slower than they really are, yet need far longer to brake.

sec11-card-f01.question_text: Why must you never dart in front of a large truck to catch an exit, turn, or single-lane work zone?
sec11-card-f01.teaching_text: Slicing across a semi's front bumper steals its braking space right where you are slowing down for an exit or taper.

sec11-card-f02.question_text: Where are the no-zone blind areas located around a truck or bus, and how does truck size affect them?
sec11-card-f02.teaching_text: Longer and taller rigs cast deeper blind zones on all four sides, especially along the right flank and close ahead.

sec11-card-f03.question_text: What quick mirror check tells you whether a truck or bus driver can actually see your car?
sec11-card-f03.teaching_text: If the cab's side mirror hides the driver's face from your eyes, your car is sitting invisible inside a no-zone.

sec11-card-f04.question_text: Why should you pass briskly rather than lingering beside a large truck or bus?
sec11-card-f04.teaching_text: Hanging next to trailer wheels leaves you trapped if wind, road debris, or a lane shift moves the rig sideways.

sec11-card-f05.question_text: Even in ideal conditions with good tires and brakes, at least how many feet does a loaded truck at fifty-five miles per hour need to stop?
sec11-card-f05.teaching_text: A loaded rig rolling fifty-five miles per hour eats more than a full football field of dry asphalt to halt.

sec11-card-f06.question_text: How does that loaded-truck stopping distance compare with the stopping distance of a passenger car?
sec11-card-f06.teaching_text: Expecting a forty-ton rig behind you to stop like a sedan guarantees a rear-end crush if you brake abruptly.

sec11-card-f07.question_text: When is it safe to pull back into the lane ahead of a large truck you just passed, and what should your speed do?
sec11-card-f07.teaching_text: Seeing the whole grille in your inside mirror—and holding steady speed—keeps you out of the front no-zone.

sec11-card-f08.question_text: How far behind a large truck or bus can its rear blind spot reach?
sec11-card-f08.teaching_text: Without a center rearview mirror through a solid trailer, a trucker cannot spot tailgaters for two hundred feet back.

sec11-card-f09.question_text: Why should you stay well back when following a large truck or bus?
sec11-card-f09.teaching_text: Tailgating a tall trailer blinds you to traffic signals and road hazards ahead while hiding you from side mirrors.

sec11-card-f10.question_text: In which two highway situations should you avoid staying in the right lane behind large trucks?
sec11-card-f10.teaching_text: Heavy rigs crawl slowly on grades and merge out of scale ramps well below freeway flow.

sec11-card-f11.question_text: How must you respond when an emergency vehicle approaches with flashing lights and a siren?
sec11-card-f11.teaching_text: Stopping right inside an intersection box traps fire trucks and ambulances that need turning room across corners.

sec11-card-f12.question_text: Once pulled over for an emergency vehicle, how long must you remain stopped?
sec11-card-f12.teaching_text: Pulling back out prematurely risks colliding with a second trailing responder unit unless an officer directs traffic.

sec11-card-f13.question_text: Which categories of stopped roadside vehicles displaying flashing lights are protected by Ohio's Move Over law?
sec11-card-f13.teaching_text: Ohio's law shields tow trucks, garbage crews, maintenance workers, and utility inspectors alongside police and ambulances.

sec11-card-f14.question_text: What is your primary duty under Ohio's Move Over law when traffic and safety allow a lane change?
sec11-card-f14.teaching_text: Putting an empty buffer lane between highway traffic and roadside workers prevents deadly shoulder sideswipes.

sec11-card-r01.question_text: What must you do for a stopped flashing-light roadside vehicle if heavy traffic makes changing lanes unsafe?
sec11-card-r01.teaching_text: Never force a blind swerve into adjacent cars—drop speed substantially and pass with heightened caution instead.

sec11-card-r02.question_text: What speed ceiling does an orange-and-red triangle on the back of farm, construction, or animal-drawn vehicles indicate?
sec11-card-r02.teaching_text: At fifty-five miles per hour you close rapidly on vehicles moving under twenty-five, so brake as soon as you spot orange.

sec11-card-r03.question_text: Where on the road must a vehicle traveling slower than normal traffic position itself?
sec11-card-r03.teaching_text: Keeping slow vehicles in the right lane or near the right edge lets normal traffic flow predictably past.

sec11-card-r04.question_text: Under what strict conditions does Ohio allow crossing a solid yellow line to pass a very slow vehicle?
sec11-card-r04.teaching_text: Notice all three conditions: the vehicle moves under half the limit, oncoming sight distance is clear, and you stay under the limit.

sec11-card-r05.question_text: What slow, wide agricultural hazards should you watch for along rural Ohio roads and state highways?
sec11-card-r05.teaching_text: Combines and wide implements often span more than one lane and pull onto highways from hidden field drives.

sec11-card-r06.question_text: Why can you not assume a tractor or combine operator hears your car approaching from behind?
sec11-card-r06.teaching_text: Heavy diesel engine roar blocks out approaching cars and horns, so watch for sudden wide left field turns.

sec11-card-r07.question_text: What two rear warning markers must farm machinery display when operating on Ohio roads at night?
sec11-card-r07.teaching_text: Spotting a single blinking red lamp ahead on a dark country road warns of creeping farm machinery.

sec11-card-r08.question_text: How does Ohio law treat the road rights and duties of horse-drawn buggies and horseback riders?
sec11-card-r08.teaching_text: Give horse-drawn buggies and riders full lane respect and calm space so loud revving or close passes never spook animals.

sec11-card-r09.question_text: How should you adjust your scanning when you pass yellow warning signs showing a buggy or horse?
sec11-card-r09.teaching_text: Cresting rural hills or rounding curves in buggy country can put a five-mile-per-hour carriage directly in your lane.

sec12-card-f01.question_text: What braking system prevents wheel-lock skids on most newer vehicles, and where do you check your car's exact braking method?
sec12-card-f01.teaching_text: Pumping anti-lock brakes defeats rapid computer pulsing, so verify your specific vehicle's braking system in the manual first.

sec12-card-f02.question_text: What is the proper steering and braking sequence when swerving around an immediate road hazard?
sec12-card-f02.teaching_text: Stomping the brake pedal mid-swerve shifts weight violently and spins the car before you straighten out.

sec12-card-f03.question_text: In which two impending-impact directions can accelerating quickly help you avoid a collision?
sec12-card-f03.teaching_text: When open space sits ahead and a car barrels toward your trunk or door, brisk gas clears the impact zone.

sec12-card-f04.question_text: What three driving or traction triggers commonly start a vehicle skid?
sec12-card-f04.teaching_text: Posted dry-road limits can still be far too fast when rain, slush, or panic braking overwhelms tire traction.

sec12-card-f05.question_text: What should your feet and hands do immediately when your vehicle starts skidding?
sec12-card-f05.teaching_text: Lifting off both pedals restores rolling tire traction while steering toward your desired path realigns the rear end.

sec12-card-f06.question_text: How must you handle a dead traffic signal in Ohio, and why do you still proceed carefully after stopping?
sec12-card-f06.teaching_text: Power-outage signals blend into dark backgrounds, so distracted cross-street drivers sometimes blow straight through without stopping.

sec12-card-f07.question_text: How should you recover safely if your wheels drop off the paved edge onto the shoulder?
sec12-card-f07.teaching_text: Jerking the wheel back onto a raised pavement lip at highway speed slingshots the car across oncoming traffic.

sec12-card-f08.question_text: What guide should you follow to keep your vehicle serviced and prevent roadside breakdowns?
sec12-card-f08.teaching_text: Routine fluid, belt, tire, and brake intervals catch worn parts in the driveway rather than in fast freeway lanes.

sec12-card-f09.question_text: If your main foot brakes fail, how should you apply the parking brake—and why?
sec12-card-f09.teaching_text: Yanking or stomping the parking brake hard locks the rear tires instantly and spins the car out of control.

sec12-card-f10.question_text: According to the Ohio handbook, what fallback steps remain if both your regular brakes and parking brake fail?
sec12-card-f10.teaching_text: Memorize Ohio's exact emergency sequence when neither brake system slows the car so you get clear and warn traffic.

sec12-card-f11.question_text: What are your first three actions if your accelerator sticks or surges uncontrollably?
sec12-card-f11.teaching_text: Shifting to neutral immediately disconnects runaway engine power from the wheels while keeping power steering alive.

sec12-card-f12.question_text: Once in neutral during an accelerator malfunction, how should you steer and brake to exit traffic?
sec12-card-f12.teaching_text: Calm steering and steady braking preserve control as you guide the coasting car onto a clear shoulder.

sec12-card-f13.question_text: After pulling safely off the road from a stuck accelerator, what final two steps secure the vehicle?
sec12-card-f13.teaching_text: Waiting until you are safely stopped off-road before cutting the ignition avoids losing power steering in live lanes.

sec12-card-f14.question_text: How does a front-tire blowout affect your vehicle's steering pull?
sec12-card-f14.teaching_text: Heavy rolling drag on a flat front steering wheel yanks the nose hard toward the blown side.

sec12-card-f15.question_text: What physical sensations tell you a rear tire—rather than a front tire—just blew out?
sec12-card-f15.teaching_text: Back-end fishtailing and vibration signal a rear flat, alongside a milder pull toward the damaged side.

sec12-card-f16.question_text: How should your hands handle the steering wheel the instant a tire blows out?
sec12-card-f16.teaching_text: Two-handed leverage fights the sudden drag pull so the car stays straight inside its lane before moving over.

sec12-card-f17.question_text: Why must you stay off the brakes right after a tire blows out, and how should you slow down?
sec12-card-f17.teaching_text: Slamming the brakes on a shredded tire locks the uneven wheel load and spins the vehicle sideways.

sec12-card-f18.question_text: Once your speed drops safely after a tire blowout, what four steps finish the roadside stop?
sec12-card-f18.teaching_text: Limping short yards to a wide level shoulder beats stopping on a blind curve or narrow bridge.

sec12-card-f19.question_text: If your engine stalls at highway speed, what happens to your steering—and can you still steer?
sec12-card-f19.teaching_text: Losing power-steering assist makes turning the wheel stiff and heavy, yet mechanical linkage still guides your front tires.

sec12-card-f20.question_text: How should you use the brake pedal to pull off the road after your engine dies?
sec12-card-f20.teaching_text: Power-brake vacuum assist runs out quickly if you pump the pedal repeatedly, so press steadily once instead.

sec12-card-f21.question_text: Once safely off the road after an engine stall, what should you try—and what two distress signals follow if it will not start?
sec12-card-f21.teaching_text: Raising the hood alongside blinking four-way flashers universally tells passing patrols and tow drivers your car is disabled.

sec12-card-f22.question_text: What is your top priority for positioning a vehicle that is breaking down?
sec12-card-f22.teaching_text: Using remaining coasting momentum to reach the shoulder prevents high-speed rear-end crashes in live travel lanes.

sec12-card-f23.question_text: Which vehicle lights should you switch on immediately to warn approaching drivers of a breakdown?
sec12-card-f23.teaching_text: Without flashing hazards, highway drivers often mistake a stopped shoulder car for moving traffic until too close.

sec12-card-f24.question_text: Roughly how far behind a broken-down vehicle should you set road flares when conditions allow?
sec12-card-f24.teaching_text: Setting warning markers well upstream alerts fast highway drivers long before curves or darkness hide your bumper.

sec12-card-f25.question_text: Where does the Ohio handbook instruct occupants to wait for help after pulling off with a breakdown?
sec12-card-f25.teaching_text: Walking along high-speed highway shoulders exposes stranded passengers to distracted or drifting traffic.

sec12-card-r01.question_text: What should you do with your car right after a crash—both when it can still drive and when it cannot?
sec12-card-r01.teaching_text: Clearing drivable cars prevents secondary pileups, while hazards and flares protect immobilized wrecks.

sec12-card-r02.question_text: After a minor fender-bender, should you leave drivable cars sitting in live lanes to wait for police?
sec12-card-r02.teaching_text: Standing between bumpers in live lanes to inspect minor dents causes far worse secondary collisions.

sec12-card-r03.question_text: How should you manage your emotions and interactions with other drivers at a crash scene?
sec12-card-r03.teaching_text: Roadside tempers escalate stress and distract everyone from traffic safety, injury checks, and accurate reporting.

sec12-card-r04.question_text: What must happen before you leave any crash scene—even if you hit an empty parked car?
sec12-card-r04.teaching_text: Driving off after scraping a parked car without leaving contact details turns a minor bump into hit-and-run.

sec12-card-r05.question_text: Once vehicles are stopped and warned at a collision scene, what immediate human check comes next?
sec12-card-r05.teaching_text: Crash adrenaline can mask bleeding or shock at first, so check every occupant before worrying about bent metal.

sec12-card-r06.question_text: Who should you call immediately whenever anyone is hurt in a traffic collision?
sec12-card-r06.teaching_text: Prompt emergency dispatch brings paramedics and traffic control to stabilize trauma and shield the roadway.

sec12-card-r07.question_text: How should you care for injured crash victims while waiting for emergency responders?
sec12-card-r07.teaching_text: Shifting an injured victim risks worsening hidden neck or spinal damage, whereas covering them fights trauma shock.

sec12-card-r08.question_text: Which three law-enforcement agencies handle crash notifications across Ohio?
sec12-card-r08.teaching_text: Reporting to the agency covering that city, county, or state route creates a documented crash report for insurers.

sec12-card-r09.question_text: What two topics should you avoid discussing with other drivers while exchanging crash details?
sec12-card-r09.teaching_text: Offhand roadside apologies or policy-limit guesses can twist liability claims before investigators review all facts.

sec12-card-r10.question_text: From which two groups of people at a crash scene should you gather names and addresses?
sec12-card-r10.teaching_text: Bystander witnesses often drive away before officers arrive, taking independent accounts of signal colors with them.

sec12-card-r11.question_text: What extra contact details must you record if the other driver was borrowing someone else's car?
sec12-card-r11.teaching_text: Auto insurance typically follows the vehicle owner, so missing an absent owner's contact stalls repair claims.

sec12-card-r12.question_text: Which three identifying details should you write down for every vehicle involved in a collision?
sec12-card-r12.teaching_text: Matching plate numbers with vehicle makes and models prevents mix-ups if a handwritten policy digit is misread.

sec12-card-r13.question_text: What three insurance-card items must drivers exchange after a collision?
sec12-card-r13.teaching_text: Writing down just a company brand name without the policy number leaves claims adjusters unable to verify coverage.

sec12-card-r14.question_text: What scene details and crash circumstances should you document while your memory is fresh?
sec12-card-r14.teaching_text: Rain, glare, construction cones, and exact event order fade fast from memory once you leave the intersection.

sec12-card-r15.question_text: With whom should you discuss the details of a crash at the scene—and with whom should you not?
sec12-card-r15.teaching_text: Giving clear facts to the investigating officer while skipping bystander chatter keeps statements accurate and calm.

sec12-card-r16.question_text: When should you contact your own auto insurance company following a collision?
sec12-card-r16.teaching_text: Prompt notice protects your policy rights even when the other driver caused the crash.

sec12-card-r17.question_text: What options fulfill your legal duty if you collide with an unattended parked vehicle?
sec12-card-r17.teaching_text: Never drive off hoping nobody saw a parking-lot scrape—either notify police or attach your required details securely.

sec12-card-r18.question_text: When and within what deadline may an Ohio driver file crash report form BMV 3303?
sec12-card-r18.teaching_text: Filing within six months alerts the Bureau of Motor Vehicles when an uninsured party causes injury or damage above four hundred dollars.
